newsitem.title: UK: Brown budget may struggle to eclipse radical Howe.
newsitem.headline: Brown budget may struggle to eclipse radical Howe.

text.p: When he presents his first budget, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown may find it hard to eclipse the radicalism of the first budget of Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in 1979.
Thatcher's first Chancellor, Geoffrey Howe, celebrated his party's return to power with a so-called "Opportunity Budget" on June 12, 1979.

He slashed income tax, financing this by increasing value added tax (VAT) to a uniform 15 percent from former dual rates of 8.0 and 12.5 percent, imposed 3.0 billion stg of spending cuts and raised official interest rates by two points to 14 percent.

Brown's plans for a windfall tax on privatised utilities, lower VAT on domestic fuel and a welfare-to-work-scheme look modest by comparison -- although he may include more radical measures such as a new 10 percent starting rate for income tax.
Thatcher's government argued that former prime minister James Callaghan's outgoing Labour government had left the economy in such a mess that draconian measures were needed.
Her advice, in her memoirs "The Downing Street Years," is that unpopular measures should be taken quickly.
"The decisive argument was that such a controversial increase in indirect taxes could only be made at the beginning of a parliament, when our mandate was fresh," she wrote.
This advice could perhaps prompt Brown to include measures such as reducing or scrapping tax relief on mortgage interest payments or reducing advance corporation tax (ACT) in his first budget.

Callaghan attacked the Howe budget as "a colossal gamble", which was unjust and inflationary. But the Conservatives went on to retain power for 18 years until Tony Blair's reborn Labour Party scored a landslide victory on May 1 this year.
They bequeathed their New Labour successors an unusually healthy economy, with steady growth, low inflation and falling unemployment.

By contrast, British inflation was running at 10 percent when the Conservatives took office in 1979, against a backdrop of surging international oil prices. Howe's budget measures added four percentage points to the retail price index.
By November 1979, RPI inflation was running at an annual 17.4 percent and money supply was still surging because of high government borrowing and strong bank lending.

The Conservatives put interest rates up again, this time to 17 percent. "Higher interest rates or lower public spending, not tinkering with fiscal demand management, were the appropriate response," Thatcher said in her memoirs.
The present Labour government faces a headline inflation rate of 2.4 percent and interest rates at 6.25 percent.
Its main economic headache is rampant consumer demand, which seems certain to provke a further monetary tightening from the Bank of England, which Brown empowered to set interest rates.
It remains to be seen whether Brown will heed Thatcher's advice that it is futile to try to use fiscal policy as the main tool to manage demand.
The Callaghan government's last full budget, on April 11, 1978, included a one percentage point rise in interest rates to 7.5 percent to try to bear down on demand.

Dennis Healey, the Chancellor, provided a net financial stimulus of 2.5 billion stg, raised tax thresholds, child benefit and retirement pensions and introduced a new tax band of 25 percent on the first 750 stg of taxable income.

Labour has abandoned much of its socialist past but Healey's comments that his budget measures were intended "to increase the incentive for greater effort and to promote social justice" would not look out of place in Brown's budget.
The political contrast between the background for the two Labour budgets could scarcely be more marked.
Blair's government enjoys a 179-seat majority in the House of Commons, the largest parliamentary majority any party has had since World War Two.

Healey's 1978 budget came in the dying days of a minority Labour government, which depended on support from the Liberal Party. Liberal dissatisfaction with the budget led to their withdrawal of support on May 25.
Callaghan staggered on but his government finally collapsed on March 29, 1979, after an attempt to impose pay restraint led to a series of devastating public sector strikes.
